title: The Winner University
statement:
Two universities report the exam scores of their students:

- `NewYork(student_id, score)`: one row per New York University student; `student_id` is unique in this table.
- `California(student_id, score)`: one row per California University student; `student_id` is unique in this table. The same id may appear in both tables; the tables are independent.

A student is **excellent** when their `score` is at least `90`. The university with more excellent students wins.

Return a single row with one column, `winner`:

- `'New York University'` when New York has more excellent students,
- `'California University'` when California has more,
- `'No Winner'` when both counts are equal (including when both are zero).
constraints: A student is excellent when score >= 90
The result always has exactly one row
reference:
WITH excellent AS (
  SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM NewYork WHERE score >= 90) AS new_york,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM California WHERE score >= 90) AS california
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN new_york > california THEN 'New York University'
    WHEN new_york < california THEN 'California University'
    ELSE 'No Winner'
  END AS winner
FROM excellent;
brute:
SELECT
  CASE SIGN(SUM(side))
    WHEN 1 THEN 'New York University'
    WHEN -1 THEN 'California University'
    ELSE 'No Winner'
  END AS winner
FROM (
  SELECT 1 AS side FROM NewYork WHERE score >= 90
  UNION ALL
  SELECT -1 AS side FROM California WHERE score >= 90
) AS votes
notes:
## Intuition

The whole answer depends on two numbers: how many New York students scored at least 90, and how many California students did. Count each with a scalar subquery, then turn the comparison of the two counts into one of three labels with `CASE`.

## Approach

1. CTE `excellent` builds a one-row table with two columns: `new_york` is `COUNT(*)` of `NewYork` rows with `score >= 90`, and `california` is the same count over `California`. Each count is its own scalar subquery, so the tables are never joined.
2. The final `SELECT` reads that single row and maps the comparison to `winner`: greater means New York, smaller means California, and anything else (equal counts) means `'No Winner'`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `NewYork` scores are 90 and 87; only 90 qualifies, so `new_york = 1`.
- `California` scores are 89 and 88; neither reaches 90, so `california = 0`.
- `excellent` is the row `(new_york = 1, california = 0)`.
- `1 > 0`, so `winner` is `'New York University'`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N + C) for N New York rows and C California rows; each table is scanned once.
- Space: O(1); the CTE holds one row.

## Pitfalls

- The threshold is inclusive: `score > 90` would miss a student who scored exactly 90 (Example 1).
- Joining the two tables before counting multiplies rows and corrupts both counts; count each table on its own.
- Counting all students instead of only excellent ones picks the bigger university, not the better one.
- Empty tables must still produce one row: `COUNT(*)` returns 0 for no rows, while `SUM` would return `null`.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `excellent` | one row with both excellent-student counts |
| `new_york` | number of `NewYork` rows with `score >= 90` |
| `california` | number of `California` rows with `score >= 90` |
| `winner` | the label chosen by comparing the two counts |

narration.1: The CTE excellent will hold one row with the two counts the answer depends on.
narration.3: A scalar subquery counts New York students whose score is at least 90.
narration.4: A second, independent subquery counts excellent California students; the tables are never joined.
narration.7: CASE turns the comparison of the two counts into one of three labels.
narration.10: Equal counts, including zero against zero, mean there is no winner.
narration.12: The final SELECT reads the single row of excellent, so the result always has exactly one row.
